Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0") or SHA1 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0") or MD5 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0") or SHA1 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0") or MD5 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

High

AI Coding Agents Found Triggering Endpoint Security Rules Built to Catch Attackers

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Sophos looked at a week of its own endpoint data and found that AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenAI Codex are setting off detection rules written to catch human intruders. The agents are not malicious. They just do a lot of things that, to a behavioral engine, look exactly like an attack. Decrypting browser credentials, listing what sits in Windows' credential store,

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] certutil-blocked-then-bitsadmin LOLBin download pivot on same host
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Claude Code launched with --dangerously-skip-permissions guardrail bypass · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — AI Coding Agents Found Triggering Endpoint Security Rules Built to Catch Attacke
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Startup-folder script drop via PowerShell (Cursor persistence pattern) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DPAPI browser-credential decrypt via PowerShell (GStack /browse skill under AI coding agent) · [LLM] Windows Credential Manager enumeration via cmdkey /list under coding agent · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
DPAPI browser-credential decrypt via PowerShell (GStack /browse skill under AI coding agent) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact PowerShell one-liner GStack's /browse skill runs under Claude Code/Cursor to unlock Chromium credential data: Add-Type System.Security then ProtectedData::Unprotect on a base64 blob. Detects browser-credential decryption regardless of whether an AI agent or an attacker drove it, while surfacing the agent parent for triage. Rationale: Uses the verbatim GStack /browse command signature from the Sophos blog (ProtectedData::Unprotect + FromBase64String under powershell), which is the highest-fidelity string in the article; the AgentLineage tag distinguishes benign agent automation from real theft without dropping either. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer's Claude Code running GStack /browse for legitimate browser automation
  • Password managers or browser-profile migration utilities that legitimately DPAPI-decrypt saved logins
  • Authorized red-team/pentest tooling exercising browser credential extraction
  • Security research or QA reproducing the Sophos finding
  • Backup/sync tooling re-protecting DPAPI blobs on the same user context
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and InitiatingProcessParentFileName — if the parent is claude.exe/cursor.exe/codex it is likely benign agent automation; confirm the logged-on user actually runs a coding agent. 2) Contain: if the parent is NOT a known agent (real theft), isolate the host and force-reset the browser-stored credentials and any SSO sessions decrypted. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for cmdkey /list, certutil/bitsadmin downloads, and startup-folder writes within the same session to separate agent noise from an intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData"
    and ProcessCommandLine has "Unprotect"
    and ProcessCommandLine has "FromBase64String"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend AgentLineage = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe","node.exe") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, AgentLineage, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has "System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData" and CommandLine has "Unprotect" and CommandLine has "FromBase64String"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| extend AgentLineage = iff(ParentProcessName has_any ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, AgentLineage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DPAPI Browser Credential Decryption via PowerShell (GStack browse skill)
id: 6f1d2a94-8c3b-4a11-9e0f-7d2c5b4a1e33
description: Detects the GStack /browse skill's PowerShell that calls DPAPI ProtectedData.Unprotect on a base64 blob to decrypt Chromium browser credentials, observed running under Claude Code/Cursor and equally used for real browser-credential theft.
references:
  - https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ai-coding-agents-found-triggering.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/08
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData'
      - 'Unprotect'
      - 'FromBase64String'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate GStack /browse browser automation by a developer's Claude Code
  - Password-manager or profile-migration tooling that decrypts DPAPI blobs
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe) @CommandLine:(*ProtectedData* AND *Unprotect* AND *FromBase64String*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/System\.Security\.Cryptography\.ProtectedData/i
| CommandLine=/Unprotect/i
| CommandLine=/FromBase64String/i
| agent := if(ParentBaseFileName=/(claude|cursor|codex|node)\.exe/i, "ai-agent", "other")
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, agent, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData*" AND Processes.process="*Unprotect*" AND Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval likely_agent=if(match(parent_process_name,"(?i)(claude|cursor|codex|node)\.exe"),"AI coding agent","other") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData*" AND Processes.process="*Unprotect*" AND Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval likely_agent=if(match(parent_process_name,"(?i)(claude|cursor|codex|node)\.exe"),"AI coding agent","other") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Windows Credential Manager enumeration via cmdkey /list under coding agent AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts cmdkey.exe /list — Claude Code was observed enumerating everything Windows Credential Manager holds. Rare in normal user space; the AI-agent parent lineage is surfaced to separate benign agent recon from an attacker's credential survey. Rationale: cmdkey.exe /list is the literal command Sophos attributed to Claude Code enumerating Credential Manager; it is uncommon enough in user space to hunt broadly while tagging agent lineage for fast triage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1555.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin auditing saved RDP / network credentials with cmdkey /list
  • Logon or provisioning scripts that inventory stored credentials
  • MDM/endpoint-management agents enumerating credential entries
  • A developer's coding agent legitimately checking cached credentials before an automation task
  • IT troubleshooting of Credential Manager / SSO issues
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain — a claude.exe/cursor.exe ancestor plus a developer user strongly implies benign agent recon; an interactive shell under a service or unexpected user warrants escalation. 2) Contain: if paired with credential decryption or exfil, isolate the host and rotate any credentials visible in Credential Manager for that user. 3) Hunt: search the same host/session for DPAPI browser decrypt (UC1), LOLBin downloads, and outbound connections to determine if enumeration led to use.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "cmdkey.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/list"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend AgentLineage = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, AgentLineage
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmdkey.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/list"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| extend AgentLineage = iff(ParentProcessName has_any ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, AgentLineage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Windows Credential Manager Enumeration via cmdkey /list
id: 2a7c9e40-1b6d-4f28-8c11-3e9a5d7b4c20
description: Detects cmdkey.exe /list enumerating stored Windows Credential Manager entries, observed under Claude Code and used by attackers for credential discovery.
references:
  - https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ai-coding-agents-found-triggering.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/08
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1555.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\cmdkey.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '/list'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Administrators auditing saved RDP/network credentials
  - Login scripts or inventory tooling listing credential entries
level: medium
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\cmdkey.exe OR *\CmdKey.exe OR *\CMDKEY.EXE) @CommandLine:*/list*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\cmdkey\.exe$/i CommandLine=/\/list/i
| agent := if(ParentBaseFileName=/(claude|cursor|codex)\.exe/i, "ai-agent", "other")
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, agent, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="cmdkey.exe" AND Processes.process="*/list*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval likely_agent=if(match(parent_process_name,"(?i)(claude|cursor|codex|node|cmd|powershell)\.exe"),"agent-or-shell","other") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="cmdkey.exe" AND Processes.process="*/list*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval likely_agent=if(match(parent_process_name,"(?i)(claude|cursor|codex|node|cmd|powershell)\.exe"),"agent-or-shell","other") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
certutil-blocked-then-bitsadmin LOLBin download pivot on same host AIDelivery High
Correlates a certutil urlcache download and a bitsadmin /transfer download on the same host within a short window — the 'retry-when-blocked' pivot Sophos flagged (OpenAI Codex fetched a python.org installer with certutil, was blocked, switched to bitsadmin). The two-tool pivot is far higher signal than either LOLBin alone. Rationale: Encodes the article's exact pivot: certutil -urlcache -split download (rule Lateral_1b) blocked, then bitsadmin /transfer (rule Exec_5a); requiring BOTH LOLBins on one host in 10m is the 'live-attacker vs static script' discriminator Sophos calls out, cutting the FP rate of either LOLBin alone. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1105 T1197
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer's coding agent (Codex/Claude) fetching a real installer from python.org and retrying with a different tool when blocked — the exact benign case in the article
  • Admin scripts that download with certutil and fall back to bitsadmin on failure
  • SCCM/BITS deployments alongside certutil cert operations
  • Software build pipelines pulling dependencies via multiple utilities
  • Legit certutil -urlcache cache-clearing runs coinciding with an unrelated BITS transfer
Suppression filter
| where not (CertCmd has_any ("python.org","aka.ms","microsoft.com") and BitsCmd has_any ("python.org","aka.ms","microsoft.com") and CertParent in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe") and BitsParent in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract both command lines and the download URLs; a signed installer from python.org/vendor CDNs under an agent parent is likely benign, an unknown/low-reputation host is not. 2) Contain: if the fetched target is untrusted, quarantine the downloaded file, block the destination, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check what executed the downloaded payload next and whether the same host also shows credential access (UC1/UC2) or startup persistence (UC4).
let window = 10m;
let certutil = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "certutil.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("urlcache","-split","http")
    | project CertTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, CertCmd=ProcessCommandLine, CertParent=InitiatingProcessFileName;
let bits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "bitsadmin.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/transfer"
    | project BitsTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, BitsCmd=ProcessCommandLine, BitsParent=InitiatingProcessFileName;
certutil
| join kind=inner bits on DeviceId
| where BitsTime between (CertTime .. CertTime + window)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project CertTime, BitsTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', BitsTime, CertTime), DeviceName, AccountName, CertCmd, BitsCmd, CertParent, BitsParent
| order by CertTime desc
let window = 10m;
let certutil = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "\\certutil.exe"
    | where CommandLine has_any ("urlcache","-split","http")
    | project CertTime=TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CertCmd=CommandLine, CertParent=ParentProcessName;
let bits = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688 and NewProcessName endswith "\\bitsadmin.exe"
    | where CommandLine has "/transfer"
    | project BitsTime=TimeGenerated, Computer, BitsCmd=CommandLine, BitsParent=ParentProcessName;
certutil
| join kind=inner bits on Computer
| where BitsTime between (CertTime .. CertTime + window)
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project CertTime, BitsTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', BitsTime, CertTime), Computer, SubjectUserName, CertCmd, BitsCmd, CertParent, BitsParent
| order by CertTime desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\certutil.exe OR *\CertUtil.exe OR *\CERTUTIL.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*urlcache* OR *-split*)) OR (@Image:(*\bitsadmin.exe OR *\BitsAdmin.exe OR *\BITSADMIN.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*/transfer*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(certutil|bitsadmin)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/urlcache|-split|\/transfer/i
| tool := if(ImageFileName=/certutil/i, "certutil", "bitsadmin")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=[count(field=tool, distinct=true, as=tool_count), collect([CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])])
| tool_count >= 2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="certutil.exe" AND (Processes.process="*urlcache*" OR Processes.process="*-split*")) OR (Processes.process_name="bitsadmin.exe" AND Processes.process="*/transfer*") by _time span=10m Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | stats dc(process_name) as tool_count values(process_name) as tools values(process) as cmdlines values(parent_process_name) as parents min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by dest user | where tool_count>=2 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime

Startup-folder script drop via PowerShell (Cursor persistence pattern) AIInstallation Medium
Detects PowerShell creating a script (.vbs/.ps1/.bat/.cmd/.js/.lnk) in the per-user Startup folder — the persistence rule Cursor tripped when it dropped Launch-EZConvert-ConsoleOnly.vbs. Writing to Startup outside a trusted installer is flagged on sight; the agent-parent lineage separates benign build helpers from real autorun implants. Rationale: Anchors on the exact persistence behavior (rule Persist_2a) and path Sophos reported for Cursor — a script written to \Start Menu\Programs\Startup\ by PowerShell — which is high-signal because trusted installers don't use PowerShell to seed Startup. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A coding agent (Cursor/Claude) legitimately creating a launcher script in Startup for a dev tool
  • Legitimate application installers that seed Startup via a PowerShell post-install step
  • User-authored login automation dropped into Startup
  • Configuration-management tooling (DSC/Intune scripts) writing startup shortcuts
  • Backup/sync software restoring a previously-present Startup script
Suppression filter
| where not (AgentLineage == "AI coding agent" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("EZConvert","build","dev"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped file's contents and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine; a benign build helper under cursor.exe differs sharply from an obfuscated launcher or one calling out to the internet. 2) Contain: if malicious, delete the Startup artifact, kill the persistence, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same PowerShell session for credential access (UC1/UC2) and LOLBin downloads (UC3), and sweep other hosts for the same Startup filename.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".ps1" or FileName endswith ".bat" or FileName endswith ".cmd" or FileName endswith ".js" or FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| extend AgentLineage = iff(InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("cursor.exe","claude.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, AgentLineage
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("vbs","ps1","bat","cmd","js","lnk")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PowerShell Writes Script to User Startup Folder
id: c4b8e6f2-9d21-4a77-b3e0-1f6c2a8d5e44
description: Detects PowerShell creating an executable script (vbs/ps1/bat/cmd/js/lnk) in the per-user Start Menu Startup folder, the persistence pattern Cursor tripped by dropping Launch-EZConvert-ConsoleOnly.vbs.
references:
  - https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ai-coding-agents-found-triggering.html

#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\/i
| TargetFileName=/\.(vbs|ps1|bat|cmd|js|lnk)$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" AND (Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.ps1" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.bat" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cmd" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.js" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where match(process_name,"(?i)(powershell|pwsh)\.exe") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" AND Filesystem.file_path="*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" AND (Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.ps1" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.bat" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cmd" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.js" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where match(process_name,"(?i)(powershell|pwsh)\.exe") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Claude Code launched with --dangerously-skip-permissions guardrail bypass AIExploitation High
Hunts any process invoked with Claude Code's --dangerously-skip-permissions flag, which Anthropic's own docs warn against and which lets the agent run without per-action approval. Sophos observed the credential-access activity running under this mode; it is a high-fidelity configuration-risk signal admins are told to block via managed settings. Rationale: The literal flag --dangerously-skip-permissions is a verbatim, unambiguous article string; it is essentially never present in legitimate managed environments, making it a clean policy-violation alert that also scopes which agent runs bypass approval. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer intentionally running Claude Code headless in a local sandbox or throwaway VM
  • CI/CD or container automation that runs the agent unattended with the flag by design
  • Security team reproducing the Sophos scenario in a lab
  • Documentation/demo of the flag being run once
  • Power user who accepted the risk on a personal dev box
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and host; confirm whether the agent then performed credential access (UC1/UC2) or downloads (UC3) in the same session. 2) Contain: enforce Anthropic managed settings to disable --dangerously-skip-permissions fleet-wide and, on corporate-data hosts, revoke the agent's blanket credential-store access. 3) Hunt: pull all hosts where the flag has appeared to gauge exposure and correlate with credential-touching detections to prioritize which sessions to investigate first.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--dangerously-skip-permissions"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "--dangerously-skip-permissions"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Claude Code Launched with --dangerously-skip-permissions

description: |

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase

            - 'DownloadString'

            - '-w hidden'

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High

ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Entra passkey enrollment vishing targets Microsoft 365 users

BleepingComputer
2026-07-08 7 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A threat actor has been targeting organizations across multiple sectors with voice-based fake security requests that ask Microsoft 365 users to enroll a new Entra passkey. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1566
Domainspasskeydeploy.com passkeyadd.com deploypasskey.com assignpasskey.com setpasskey.com

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Pink (O-UNC-066) Entra passkey vishing — connection to passkey-themed phishing domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Attacker-controlled Entra passkey (FIDO2) registration after off-pattern sign-in
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Pink post-compromise SharePoint/OneDrive bulk download (data extortion staging)
Pink (O-UNC-066) Entra passkey vishing — connection to passkey-themed phishing domains AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS/web traffic to the operator-controlled passkey-enrollment phishing domains used by O-UNC-066 / Pink, and to any external host whose name contains 'passkey' that is not a Microsoft property. These domains front the PHP relay panel that steers victims through /gate, /identify, /password and /passkey/register. Rationale: Uses the five article-named phishing domains (all confirmed in Okta's own write-up) plus a 'passkey'-in-host heuristic that excludes legitimate Microsoft enrollment endpoints — legitimate Entra passkey registration never traverses a third-party domain literally named *passkey*. Domain names are DNS-lowercased so no case enumeration is needed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/en-nl/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/01/23/okta-vishing-adaptable-phishing-kits/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security vendor or password-manager blog article with 'passkey' in the URL being read by an employee
  • Internal test/staging host named e.g. passkey-portal.corp.example that is not a Microsoft domain
  • Legitimate third-party passwordless IdP whose portal subdomain contains 'passkey'
  • Threat-intel analyst or this very detection team browsing the malicious domains for research
  • Marketing/SaaS newsletters linking to passkey-branded landing pages
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe")) and not(Host in~ ("passkey-portal.corp.local"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/device that resolved the domain; check whether they received an inbound phone call in the prior 30 min (vishing lure) and whether a browser process (msedge/chrome) initiated the connection. 2) Contain: force-revoke the user's Entra sessions (revokeSignInSessions), reset the password, and immediately review Authentication Methods for any FIDO2/passkey added in the last 24h (see companion UC). 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolved IP across all hosts, pull EmailUrlInfo/SMS gateway logs for the domain, and check SharePoint/OneDrive download volume for the same account.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| extend Host = tolower(tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host))
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("passkeydeploy.com","passkeyadd.com","assignpasskey.com","deploypasskey.com","setpasskey.com")
   or (Host has "passkey" and not(Host endswith "microsoft.com") and not(Host endswith "microsoftonline.com") and not(Host endswith "msftauth.net") and not(Host endswith "windows.net"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadDomains = dynamic(["passkeydeploy.com","passkeyadd.com","assignpasskey.com","deploypasskey.com","setpasskey.com"]);
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| extend q = tolower(Name)
| where q has_any (BadDomains)
   or (q has "passkey" and not(q endswith "microsoft.com") and not(q endswith "microsoftonline.com") and not(q endswith "msftauth.net") and not(q endswith "windows.net"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Attacker-controlled Entra passkey (FIDO2) registration after off-pattern sign-in AIInstallation High
Detects registration of a FIDO2 security key / passkey on an Entra account where the registration is preceded, within 6 hours, by a successful sign-in from an IP different to the one performing the registration — the exact persistence step O-UNC-066 performs after relaying credentials/MFA through its PHP panel. The BIP-39 recovery-phrase screen shown to the victim is decoy; the passkey being registered is the attacker's. Rationale: The article's core novel behaviour is an attacker registering a passkey they control while distracting the victim with a fake BIP-39 phrase. Microsoft's audit docs confirm FIDO2/passkey enrollment emits 'registered security info' / 'Add Passkey' operations via the Authentication Methods service; correlating with a differing-IP recent sign-in separates campaign activity from legitimate self-enrollment. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/en-nl/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-passkeys-fido2 • https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/coreinfrastructureandsecurityblog/auditing-fido2-authentication-for-windows-sign-in/4509702
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1556.006
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate admin-run Entra 'passkey registration campaign' (the exact feature the attacker abuses) driving genuine self-enrollments
  • Roaming/VPN user whose sign-in IP differs from the IP that hit the passkey registration endpoint
  • Helpdesk-assisted passkey enrollment where an admin registers on behalf of a user
  • Employee enrolling a new FIDO2 key from home after a corporate-network sign-in earlier the same day
  • Mobile-then-desktop enrollment where two devices produce two IPs
Suppression filter
| where RegIP !in ("<approved-enrollment-egress-ips-not-used-here>") // instead maintain a watchlist: | join kind=leftanti (_GetWatchlist('ApprovedPasskeyEnrollmentIPs') | project RegIP = SearchKey) on RegIP
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the tenant is running an approved passkey campaign; inspect the RegIP against the user's known ISPs/countries and the AppDisplayName used. 2) Contain: if unexpected, remove the newly registered FIDO2 method via Entra Authentication Methods, revoke sessions, reset credentials, and require re-enrollment from a managed device. 3) Hunt: check SharePoint/OneDrive bulk downloads for the account (companion UC), review other users who registered passkeys from the same RegIP/ASN in the last 30 days, and look for the phishing-domain resolutions from that user's device.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info", "Add Passkey", "User registered security info", "Admin registered security info")
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("FIDO2", "passkey", "Passkey", "fido2")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, Application, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
let win = 6h;
let Signins = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | extend SigninCountry = tostring(parse_json(tostring(LocationDetails)).countryOrRegion)
    | project SigninTime = TimeGenerated, UPN = UserPrincipalName, SigninIP = IPAddress, SigninCountry, AppDisplayName;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where LoggedByService == "Authentication Methods"
| where OperationName has_any ("registered security info", "Add Passkey")
| where tostring(AdditionalDetails) has_any ("FIDO2", "passkey", "Passkey") or tostring(TargetResources) has_any ("FIDO2", "passkey")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), RegIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| where isnotempty(Actor)
| join kind=inner Signins on $left.Actor == $right.UPN
| where SigninTime between (TimeGenerated - win .. TimeGenerated)
| where isnotempty(RegIP) and SigninIP != RegIP
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, OperationName, RegIP, SigninTime, SigninIP, SigninCountry, AppDisplayName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Entra Passkey (FIDO2) Security Info Registration
id: 2d7b9a10-3c4e-4f5a-8b6c-9d0e1f2a3b4c
description: A FIDO2 security key / passkey was registered as an Entra authentication method — the persistence step in O-UNC-066 / Pink passkey vishing. Triage against expected enrollment source/user.
references:

  - https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/concept-authentication-passkeys-fido2
author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:

detection:

source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:("User registered security info" OR "Admin registered security info" OR "Add Passkey (device-bound)")
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.action="modified" AND All_Changes.command IN ("User registered security info","Admin registered security info","Add Passkey (device-bound)") by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.object, All_Changes.command | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | search object="*FIDO2*" OR object="*passkey*" OR command="Add Passkey*" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.action="modified" AND All_Changes.command IN ("User registered security info","Admin registered security info","Add Passkey (device-bound)") by All_Changes.user, All_Changes.src, All_Changes.object, All_Changes.command | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | search object="*FIDO2*" OR object="*passkey*" OR command="Add Passkey*" | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Pink post-compromise SharePoint/OneDrive bulk download (data extortion staging) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single Entra account downloading an anomalously high volume of files from SharePoint and OneDrive in a short window — the rapid data-theft step Okta/Unit 42 attribute to Pink immediately after account takeover, feeding their extortion leak site. Article-specific because Pink 'moves quickly to exfiltrate from SharePoint and OneDrive' right after passkey-based access. Rationale: Threshold on FileDownloaded/FileSyncDownloadedFull scoped to SharePoint+OneDrive captures the bulk-collection step the article and Unit 42 attribute to Pink; per-user hourly bucketing plus IP fan-out lets an analyst separate a compromised account (new IP, huge burst) from a heavy legitimate user. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/en-nl/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/
ATT&CKT1213.002 T1530
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee offboarding / bulk archival of their own OneDrive before departure
  • OneDrive Known Folder Move re-sync onto a newly provisioned laptop
  • Data-migration or eDiscovery export tooling running under a service account
  • Legitimate power user pulling a large document library for an offline project
  • Backup/DLP agent enumerating and downloading files
Suppression filter
| where UserId !endswith "$" and UserId !in~ ("svc-migration@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com", "eDiscoveryExport@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the download burst IP with the account's normal sign-in IPs and with any FIDO2/passkey added in the prior 24h (companion UC); check if downloads span many distinct sites/libraries (theft) vs one folder (legit). 2) Contain: disable the account, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, and block the source IP; preserve OfficeActivity for the window. 3) Hunt: search the extortion pattern across other accounts sharing that IP/ASN, review outbound uploads to file-sharing/cloud services from those sessions, and confirm no attacker passkey persists.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application in ("Microsoft SharePoint Online", "Microsoft OneDrive for Business")
| where ActionType in ("FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloadedFull", "FileDownloadedProtected")
| summarize FileCount = count(), Files = make_set(ObjectName, 50), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where FileCount > 100    // 100 = P99 hourly download volume for a single interactive user in most tenants; tune to local baseline
| order by FileCount desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload in ("SharePoint", "OneDrive")
| where Operation in ("FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloadedFull")
| summarize FileCount = count(), UniqueFiles = dcount(SourceFileName), IPs = make_set(ClientIP, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where FileCount > 100    // 100 = P99 hourly single-user download volume; tune to local baseline
| order by FileCount desc
CLOUD
index=o365 sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Workload IN ("SharePoint","OneDrive") Operation IN ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull") | bin _time span=1h | stats count as FileCount dc(SourceFileName) as UniqueFiles values(ClientIP) as ClientIPs values(SourceRelativeUrl) as Paths by UserId, _time | where FileCount > 100
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject

     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]

         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60

New HalluSquatting Attack Could Trick AI Coding Assistants Into Installing Botnet Malware

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 9 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

AI coding assistants have a habit of making things up. Ask one to fetch a popular tool, and it will sometimes hand back a real-sounding name for a project that does not exist. New research, which its authors call&nbsp;HalluSquatting, turns that habit into an attack: work out the fake names an AI reliably invents, register them first, and wait for the assistant to fetch your trap on a user's
